title: Conditional Compilation Scattered Through Functional Logic
pattern: Platform, hardware, provider, or mock variants are implemented by interleaving conditional-compilation branches (`#[cfg(...)]` in Rust, `#ifdef` in C/C++) inside business or functional logic instead of isolating cohesive implementations.
why_bad: Readers must mentally reconstruct multiple compilation paths at once, adding a new variant requires hunting down and editing scattered branch flags, and inactive branches are invisible to the compiler, hiding compilation errors and complicating test coverage and static analysis.
detection: Look for `#[cfg(...)]` blocks or `#ifdef`-style checks inside function or method bodies, particularly when they enclose line-by-line alternative logic. Also flag the exact same hardware/environment feature flag (e.g., `#[cfg(feature = "...")]`) appearing repeatedly inside multiple functional bodies rather than at module boundaries. Inline placement is a review signal; determine whether these are avoidable business-level alternatives or necessary low-level platform code.
source: *Robert C. Martin - Clean Code (2008)*, Chapter 3, "Functions"; *Titus Winters et al. - Software Engineering at Google (2020)*, Chapter 14, "Larger Testing" (Configuration vs Code); *Clean Architecture*, Chapter 20: "Business Rules" — "DRY", p. 272; [Robert C. Martin Series] Robert C. Martin - *Clean Architecture_ A Craftsman’s Guide to Software Structure and Design* (2017, Prentice Hall).pdf, Chapter 28; [Robert C. Martin series] Feathers, Michael C - *Working effectively with legacy code* (2013, Prentice Hall PTR).pdf, Chapter 21.
